catalog_locator: Section 4 'Stress', rules 4.1-4.2, pp. 32-33 (pp. 4-5); also section 2 p. 30, section 9 p. 42 (p. 14: 'Roots of more than one syllable have stress on their penultimate syllable', [hilgúki]) and p. 44 (p. 16: 'single-syllable roots, which always retain at least secondary stress'), endnotes 8-9 p. 55; cross-check Fields 1997 p. 239
catalog_quote: Stress in Orya is non-phonemic and has the function of highlighting word roots and endings in the stream of speech. Stress may be accompanied by a little length as well, especially on word roots. 4.1 Primary stress occurs on the penultimate syllable of a word root. When the root is followed by a one-syllable suffix, the original stress does not change. When two or more syllables are suffixed to a root, the penultimate syllable receives primary stress and the root retains secondary stress. ... (Primary stress is underlined in examples in this section ...) /bó.ton/ false /bó.ton-.gwek/ she lied /bó.ton-.gwé.ka/ he lied /en.lá.la/ thought (NOUN) /en.lá.la-.gwek/ I thought /en.lá.la-.gwé.ʔan/ I'm thinking /en.lá.la-.gwe.bíl.nan/ I've been thinking about it ... 4.2 Primary stress always precedes two sonorant consonantals (/n/, /m/, /ŋ/ and /l/) if these occur on the penultimate or antepenultimate syllables. ... According to the first stress rule, primary stress will not change if a single-syllable suffix is added to a root. This second rule, however, will cause a change in primary stress if the adding of the suffix results in two sonorant consonantals coming together. ... This rule also causes normal penultimate stress to become antepenultimate. ... /bálk-gul.lá.da/ -----> [balkgúluda] he caught her ... When the two front sonorants are farther from the end of the word than the antepenultimate syllable, the stress is not changed.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable (non-contrastive). Bare roots are stressed on their penult; a root plus one monosyllabic suffix keeps the root's stress (so stress can sit on the word antepenult); with two or more suffix syllables primary stress moves to the penultimate syllable of the whole word and the root keeps secondary stress. A cluster of two sonorant consonants on the penult/antepenult attracts primary stress to the preceding vowel, which can yield antepenultimate stress. Fields 1997:239 summarises simply: 'Orya is pronounced with penultimate stress.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Root retains secondary stress when primary stress moves to the word penult under 2+ suffix syllables; single-syllable roots always keep at least secondary stress (relevant to vowel harmony, section 9).
new_statements.exceptions: (a) Root + single monosyllabic suffix: root-penult stress unchanged (e.g. /bó.ton-gwek/ 'she lied' vs /bo.ton-gwé.kal/ 'he lied'); (b) rule 4.2 double-sonorant attraction makes normal penultimate stress antepenultimate (e.g. [bálkuiluda] 'he caught her'); not applied when the sonorant cluster is further left than the antepenult; (c) frequent compounds like /en-lala/ 'think' count as roots for stress (endnote 9); monosyllabic words are stressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated over root + suffixes (the verb complex is phonologically one word); section 2 separately describes sentence/pause-group intonation with a pitch rise on the stressed, usually penultimate, syllable. Dialect described: Guay.
new_statements.identity_note: Fields 1991 describes the Guay dialect of Orya (Unurum-Guay district, Kabupaten Jayapura); language-level glottocode orya1242, no separate dialect code. Older name in government records/Voorhoeve: Uria.

new_statements.quote: [PDF p.7, 'Orya Phonology':] A phonological analysis of Orya has been published.vii Orya is pronounced with penultimate stress, and the orthography closely matches a phonetic representation. [endnote vii, PDF p.54:] Fields 1991 [PDF p.18, 'Case and question phrases':] The question word is typically placed after the actor/subject noun phrase. There is usually some extra stress on the question word, and no rising intonation at the end of the sentence.

new_statements.relation_note: Same author, same Guay variety; the 2000 summary restates the placement as plain 'penultimate stress' (word for word the note in Fields 1997 p.239 already held by the project) and cites Fields 1991 (endnote vii), the catalog's source, for the full analysis. It omits the catalog record's morphological detail (primary stress on the penult of the ROOT, unchanged under a one-syllable suffix; word-penult primary with root secondary when 2+ syllables are suffixed; 4.2 sonorant attraction) but states nothing that conflicts with it, so it neither refines nor contradicts; the existing statement's reading 'fixed: penultimate syllable' is matched exactly. No tone claim.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Orya falls on the penultimate syllable; the summary gives only this one-line statement (with an orthography that is near-phonetic) and refers the compiler to the published phonology, Fields 1991, for the analysis. Separately, in questions the question word carries extra (phrasal) stress and there is no sentence-final rising intonation. Nothing on tone; no weight conditions; no statement of the stress domain (root vs word) in this work.
new_statements.secondary_stress: not mentioned in this work (the root-secondary-stress rule under 2+ suffix syllables is only in Fields 1991, sections 4.1-4.2).
new_statements.exceptions: none for word stress; only the phrase-level note that question words take extra stress and questions lack final rising intonation (p.18).
new_statements.identity_note: Orya [ury], Tor-Orya, Papua (Indonesia); Fields' SIL fieldwork variety, same author and language as the catalog source Fields 1991.
